'''Walter William Rouse Ball'''{{efn|Pronounced {{IPAc-en|ˈ|w|ɔː|l|.|t|ər|_|ˈ|w|ɪ|l|.|j|ə|m|_|r|aʊ|s|_|b|ɔː|l}}; that is, ''Rouse'' rhymes with ''mouse'', unlike the ordinary word ''rouse''.}} (14 August 1850 – 4 April 1925), known as '''W.&nbsp;W. Rouse Ball''', was a British [[mathematician]], lawyer, and fellow at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], from 1878 to 1905. He was also a keen amateur magician, and the founding president of the Cambridge [[Pentacle Club]] in 1919, one of the world's oldest magic societies.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://geniimagazine.com/wiki/index.php?title=Pentacle_Club&redirect=no|title=Pentacle Club – Magicpedia|access-date=3 November 2009|archive-date=20 November 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231120210600/http://geniimagazine.com/wiki/index.php?title=Pentacle_Club&redirect=no|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=whittaker>{{cite journal |last1=Whittaker |first1=E.&nbsp;T. | author-link1 =E. T. Whittaker |date=October 1925 |title=Obituary: W. W. Rouse Ball |jstor=3604492 |journal=[[The Mathematical Gazette]] |volume=12 |issue=178 |pages=449–454 |doi=10.1017/S0025557200247207 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Life==
Born 14 August 1850 in [[Hampstead]], [[London]], Ball was the son and heir of Walter Frederick Ball, of 3, St John's Park Villas, South Hampstead, London. Educated at [[University College School]], he entered [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], in 1870, became a scholar and first [[Smith's Prize]]man, and gained his BA in 1874 as second [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Wrangler]]. He became a Fellow of Trinity in 1875, and remained one for the rest of his life.<ref>{{acad|id=BL870WW|name=Ball, Walter William Rouse}}</ref>

He died on 4 April 1925 in Elmside, [[Cambridge]],<ref name=whittaker/> and is buried at the [[Ascension Parish Burial Ground, Cambridge|Parish of the Ascension Burial Ground]] in Cambridge.<ref>{{cite book
| last=Singmaster
| first=David
| chapter=1892 Walter William Rouse Ball, Mathematical recreations and problems of past and present times
| pages=653–663
| editor-last=Grattan-Guinness
| editor-first=I.
| title=Landmark Writings in Western Mathematics 1640–1940
| year=2005
| publisher=Elsevier
| isbn=978-0-444-50871-3
}} See p. 658.</ref>

He is commemorated in the naming of the small pavilion, now used as changing rooms and toilets, on [[Jesus Green]] in Cambridge.
